new-year.detail:
The first day of Muharram opens the Hijri year. The Islamic calendar is lunar: each month begins with the new crescent, so the year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year.

The calendar was organised under the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, some years after the death of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The Companions chose to count the years from the Hijra, the emigration of the Prophet ﷺ from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, and to keep Muharram as the first month. The Hijra itself took place later in the year, in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal.

Muharram is one of the four sacred months mentioned in the Qur'an (9:36). The Prophet ﷺ taught that the best fast after Ramadan is the fast of Allah's month, Muharram (Sahih Muslim 1163).

No special prayer or celebration is prescribed for this day. Many Muslims simply use it to remember the Hijra, look back on the past year and make good resolutions.

tasua.detail:
Tasu'a is the ninth day of Muharram, the day before Ashura.

When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ fasted Ashura and told the Muslims to fast it, his Companions pointed out that Jews and Christians also honoured that day. He answered that the following year, if Allah willed, they would fast the ninth as well. He passed away before the next Muharram came (Sahih Muslim 1134).

For this reason, scholars recommend fasting the ninth together with the tenth. This gives the Muslim fast its own form while keeping the link with the day on which Allah saved Moses (peace be upon him).

This fast is voluntary. Someone who can only fast the tenth still fasts Ashura, and nobody who is ill, travelling or unable to fast should feel guilty. Muharram as a whole is a sacred month, and the Prophet ﷺ taught that fasting in it is the best fast after Ramadan (Sahih Muslim 1163).

ashura.detail:
Ashura is the tenth day of Muharram. Its story goes back to Moses (peace be upon him): on this day Allah saved him and the Children of Israel from their enemy.

When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to Medina, he found the Jews fasting on this day in memory of that rescue. He said that the Muslims had more right to Moses, so he fasted it and told the Muslims to fast it (Sahih al-Bukhari 2004). When the fast of Ramadan became obligatory, fasting Ashura remained a voluntary, recommended act (Sahih al-Bukhari 2002).

Asked about its reward, the Prophet ﷺ said that it expiates the sins of the past year (Sahih Muslim 1162). It is recommended to fast the ninth day along with it (Sahih Muslim 1134).

Ashura is also the day on which al-Husayn ibn Ali, the grandson of the Prophet ﷺ, was killed at Karbala in the year 61 of the Hijra (680 CE), a painful memory for Muslims.

mawlid.detail:
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born in Mecca, in the clan of Banu Hashim of the tribe of Quraysh, in the year known as the Year of the Elephant, around 570 CE. His father Abdullah died before his birth, and his mother Amina died when he was a small child.

It is established that he was born on a Monday: asked about fasting on Mondays, he said it was the day he was born and the day revelation came to him (Sahih Muslim 1162). Most historians place his birth in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal. The 12th is the best-known date, but other days have been suggested and none is certain.

Muslims differ about marking this day. Many gather to recall his life, send blessings upon him and share food. Others do not single the day out, because the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions did not do so. All agree on loving him and following his example every day; the Qur'an describes him as a mercy to the worlds (21:107).

isra-miraj.detail:
Al-Isra is the night journey of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ from the Sacred Mosque in Mecca to al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. The Qur'an mentions it at the opening of Surah al-Isra (17:1). Al-Mi'raj is his ascension from there through the heavens, where he met earlier prophets (peace be upon them) and was shown great signs of his Lord; Surah an-Najm alludes to this (53:13-18).

It happened in Mecca, before the Hijra, in a period of hardship for the Prophet ﷺ. The most lasting gift of that night is the five daily prayers, which were made obligatory then (Sahih al-Bukhari 349).

The exact date is not known with certainty. The 27th of Rajab is the date most commonly remembered, but early historians mention other dates.

No particular prayer or fast is established for this night. Many Muslims use the occasion to retell the event and to remember the value of the prayer; others do not mark the date. Rajab is one of the four sacred months (9:36).

mid-shaban.detail:
Sha'ban is the eighth month, just before Ramadan. Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) reported that she never saw the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ fast in any month, apart from Ramadan, as much as he did in Sha'ban (Sahih al-Bukhari 1969). It is a month for getting ready: voluntary fasts, making up fasts missed in the previous Ramadan, and reading the Qur'an.

The night of the 15th, in the middle of the month, is known in many countries by names such as Laylat al-Bara'a, Shab-e-Barat or Nisfu Sya'ban. Several reports speak of Allah's forgiveness on this night. Scholars differ about how strong these reports are, and so they differ about the practice: many Muslims spend part of the night in prayer and supplication and fast during the day; others treat it like any other night of Sha'ban and do not set aside special worship for it.

What is agreed is that asking for forgiveness, mending relations with others and voluntary fasting are good throughout Sha'ban, the doorway to Ramadan.

ramadan-start.detail:
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Hijri year, the month in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for people (2:185). Fasting during it is one of the five pillars of Islam (Sahih al-Bukhari 8). It was prescribed in Medina, in the second year after the Hijra.

The month begins when the new crescent is sighted; if it cannot be seen, Sha'ban is completed as thirty days (Sahih al-Bukhari 1909). This is why the start may differ by a day from one country to another.

From dawn to sunset, those who fast give up food, drink and marital relations. The sick and travellers are exempt and make up the days later, and those who cannot fast at all feed a poor person instead (2:184-185). The Qur'an gives the aim of the fast: to grow in God-consciousness (2:183).

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that when Ramadan begins, the gates of heaven are opened, the gates of Hell are closed and the devils are chained (Sahih al-Bukhari 1899). It is a month of prayer, Qur'an and generosity.

last-ten-nights.detail:
The last ten nights of Ramadan begin on the evening before the 21st day and run to the end of the month, which has 29 or 30 days. They are the most precious part of Ramadan, because Laylat al-Qadr is among them.

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) reported that when these ten began, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would tighten his belt, spend the night in prayer and wake his family (Sahih al-Bukhari 2024). He strove in worship in these nights more than at any other time (Sahih Muslim 1175).

He also practised i'tikaf, staying in the mosque to devote himself to worship, during the last ten days of Ramadan until he died (Sahih al-Bukhari 2026).

What is recommended: night prayer, reading the Qur'an, plenty of supplication, asking forgiveness and charity. Those who cannot stay up for long can still pray a little each night, so that they do not miss the night that is better than a thousand months (97:3). Zakat al-fitr is also prepared in these days, before the Eid prayer.

laylat-al-qadr.detail:
Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree, is the night in which the Qur'an was sent down. A whole surah is devoted to it: it is better than a thousand months, the angels and the Spirit descend in it by their Lord's permission, and it is peace until the rising of dawn (97:1-5). The Qur'an also calls it a blessed night (44:3).

Its exact date has been kept hidden. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told the believers to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan (Sahih al-Bukhari 2017): the 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th or 29th. The 27th is the night most often mentioned, and many communities gather on it, but it is not certain, and scholars hold different views. The wisest course is to make an effort on all ten nights.

The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever stands in prayer on Laylat al-Qadr with faith and hoping for reward will have his past sins forgiven (Sahih al-Bukhari 2014). Recommended acts are night prayer, reciting the Qur'an, supplication and asking Allah for pardon.

eid-al-fitr.detail:
Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, falls on the first day of Shawwal and closes the month of Ramadan. The Qur'an asks the believers to complete the number of days and to glorify Allah for having guided them (2:185).

Before the Eid prayer, zakat al-fitr is given: a small charity of staple food, due for every member of the household, so that the poor can share in the day. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ ordered it to be paid before people go out to the prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari 1503).

In the morning, Muslims say the takbir, wear their best clothes and gather for the Eid prayer, which is followed by a sermon (Sahih al-Bukhari 956). The Prophet ﷺ would not leave for the prayer on this day until he had eaten some dates (Sahih al-Bukhari 953).

Fasting on the day of Eid is not permitted (Sahih al-Bukhari 1991). It is a day of thanks, family visits and kindness to neighbours. Voluntary fasts, such as the six days of Shawwal, can start from the second day.

six-shawwal.detail:
Shawwal is the month that follows Ramadan. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six days of Shawwal, it is as if he had fasted the whole year (Sahih Muslim 1164).

Scholars explain this with the rule that a good deed is rewarded ten times over (6:160): the month of Ramadan counts as ten months, and six more days count as two months, which makes a full year.

Any six days of the month count. The app shows the 2nd to the 7th only as a convenient range: the days may be fasted one after another or spread out, at the beginning, middle or end of Shawwal. The only day excluded is the 1st, the day of Eid, when fasting is not permitted.

This fast is voluntary, not an obligation. Someone who still has days of Ramadan to make up should plan for them too: many scholars advise making them up first, while others allow the six days before. It is a gentle way to keep the good habits of Ramadan alive.

dhul-hijja-nine.detail:
Dhul-Hijja is the twelfth month, the month of the Hajj. Its first ten days are among the best days of the year: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that no good deeds are better than those done in these days (Sahih al-Bukhari 969). Many commentators also understand the ten nights by which Allah swears in the Qur'an (89:2) as referring to them.

Since fasting is one of the best deeds, it is recommended to fast during the first nine days, as much as one can. The ninth, the Day of Arafat, is the most emphasised. The tenth is Eid al-Adha, when fasting is not permitted.

Other recommended acts are to repeat the takbir, to praise Allah often, to pray, to give charity and to read the Qur'an. The Qur'an speaks of mentioning Allah's name on known days (22:28).

Whoever intends to offer a sacrifice is told not to cut his hair or nails from the start of the month until the sacrifice is done (Sahih Muslim 1977). During these days, pilgrims from all over the world gather in Mecca.

arafat.detail:
The ninth of Dhul-Hijja is the Day of Arafat, the heart of the Hajj. From midday until sunset the pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafat, near Mecca, in prayer and supplication. Standing at Arafat is the essential pillar of the pilgrimage.

It was on this day, a Friday, during the Farewell Pilgrimage of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, that the verse announcing that Allah had perfected the religion was revealed (5:3), as Umar ibn al-Khattab reported (Sahih al-Bukhari 45).

The Prophet ﷺ said that there is no day on which Allah frees more servants from the Fire than the Day of Arafat (Sahih Muslim 1348).

For those who are not on Hajj, fasting this day is strongly recommended: the Prophet ﷺ said that it expiates the sins of the previous year and of the coming year (Sahih Muslim 1162). The pilgrims themselves are not asked to fast; the Prophet ﷺ did not fast while standing at Arafat (Sahih al-Bukhari 1988).

It is a day for supplication, remembrance of Allah and seeking forgiveness, wherever one is.

eid-al-adha.detail:
Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, falls on the tenth of Dhul-Hijja, the day after Arafat. It coincides with the main rites of the Hajj at Mina and Mecca.

It recalls the trial of Abraham (peace be upon him). He saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son; both submitted to Allah's command, and Allah ransomed the son with a great sacrifice (37:102-107).

The day begins with the Eid prayer, followed by a sermon (Sahih al-Bukhari 956). After the prayer, those who are able sacrifice a sheep, a goat, a cow or a camel. The meat is eaten by the family, offered to relatives and neighbours and given to the poor. The Qur'an reminds believers that neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah; what reaches Him is their piety (22:37).

Fasting is not permitted on this day (Sahih al-Bukhari 1991). Muslims say the takbir, wear their best clothes, visit one another and share food. The sacrifice may also be made on the days that follow.

tashriq.detail:
The days of Tashriq are the 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhul-Hijja, the three days after Eid al-Adha. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described them as days of eating, drinking and remembrance of Allah (Sahih Muslim 1141).

During these days the pilgrims stay at Mina and throw pebbles at the three pillars called the jamarat each day. The Qur'an tells them to remember Allah during these numbered days, and says that there is no sin on whoever hurries to leave after two days, nor on whoever stays longer (2:203). So pilgrims may leave on the 12th or stay until the 13th.

Fasting on these days is not permitted. The only exception reported is for pilgrims who owe a sacrificial offering and cannot find one (Sahih al-Bukhari 1997).

For everyone else, these are days of joy and gratitude: sharing the meat of the sacrifice, visiting relatives and saying the takbir, especially after the daily prayers. The Eid sacrifice may still be offered in these days, with details that vary between the schools of law.
